title: Custom Middleware
description: Learn to write reusable custom middleware classes in ASP.NET Core, configure them with dependency injection, and understand the difference between inline and class-based middleware.

blocks.text: While built-in middleware handles many common scenarios, you will often need custom logic that is specific to your application. Custom middleware gives you a clean, reusable way to implement cross-cutting concerns like request logging, response compression, tenant resolution, or feature flags.

Custom middleware can be written as inline lambdas for simple one-off logic, or as dedicated classes for reusable, testable components. Class-based middleware supports dependency injection, making it the preferred approach for anything beyond trivial logic.

Inline middleware uses a lambda expression passed to app.Use(). It is quick to write and great for small pieces of logic in a single application. However, inline middleware has limitations: it cannot use dependency injection for its dependencies, and it is harder to test in isolation.

blocks.title: When to use each approach
items: Use inline middleware (app.Use) for quick, simple logic that does not require injected services
Use class-based middleware when you need constructor-injected dependencies like ILogger<T> or IConfiguration
Use class-based middleware when the logic is complex enough to deserve its own test class
Use class-based middleware when you want to share the same middleware across multiple projects

blocks.text: A class-based middleware must accept a RequestDelegate in its constructor and expose a method called InvokeAsync or Invoke that takes an HttpContext and returns a Task. Dependencies are injected through the constructor.

blocks.title: Request logging middleware class
blocks.content: A reusable middleware class that logs request details using ILogger, injected via the constructor.

blocks.text: The constructor receives both the next delegate (injected by the framework) and any other services you need. The InvokeAsync method does the actual work: logging the request before next(), and logging the response status after next() returns.

blocks.title: Important: Middleware constructor lifetime
blocks.text: Middleware classes are created once at application startup, not per-request. Any services you inject into the constructor must be safe to share across requests. Do not inject scoped services like DbContext into the middleware constructor — only into InvokeAsync if needed.

Once you have a middleware class, you register it in Program.cs using the UseMiddleware<T>() extension method. The framework resolves dependencies from the service provider and passes them to your constructor.

blocks.title: Registering custom middleware in Program.cs
blocks.content: Register the RequestLoggingMiddleware class in the pipeline.

blocks.text: When you call UseMiddleware<RequestLoggingMiddleware>(), ASP.NET Core automatically resolves RequestDelegate for the constructor. You do not need to manually register RequestDelegate in the service collection.

blocks.title: Info: Middleware activation
blocks.text: ASP.NET Core uses a special middleware activator that can resolve RequestDelegate and ILogger<T> without explicit registration. Other dependencies like IConfiguration or custom services still need to be registered in the service collection.
For middleware that needs configuration, you can use the options pattern. Create a class to hold settings, register it with Configure<TOptions>, and inject IOptions<TOptions> into your middleware.

blocks.title: Middleware with configuration options
blocks.content: A rate-limiting middleware that reads allowed requests from configuration.

blocks.text: The options pattern decouples your middleware from configuration sources. You can load settings from appsettings.json, environment variables, or any other configuration provider, and the middleware receives them through IOptions<RateLimitOptions>.

terms.definition: A delegate that represents the next middleware in the pipeline. Every middleware receives it as a constructor parameter.
The method on a class-based middleware that processes the request and optionally calls the next delegate.
The extension method that registers a class-based middleware in the pipeline.
A pattern for binding configuration values to strongly-typed classes, injected via IOptions<T>.
When middleware returns a response without calling next(), stopping the remaining pipeline from executing.

blocks.title: Middleware that adds a response header
blocks.content: A simple middleware that injects a custom header into every outgoing response.

blocks.title: Create a Correlation ID Middleware
blocks.description: Build a class-based middleware that generates a unique correlation ID for each request, adds it to the response headers, and logs it alongside the request path.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core MVC project named 'CorrelationDemo'
Add a new class 'CorrelationIdMiddleware' with a constructor accepting RequestDelegate and ILogger<CorrelationIdMiddleware>
In InvokeAsync, check if the incoming request has an 'X-Correlation-ID' header; if not, generate a new GUID
Add the correlation ID to context.Response.Headers using OnStarting so it is set before the response is sent
Log the correlation ID and request path using _logger.LogInformation
Register the middleware in Program.cs using UseMiddleware<CorrelationIdMiddleware>()
Run the app and use curl to verify the X-Correlation-ID header appears in every response
blocks.expectedOutcome: Every HTTP response includes an X-Correlation-ID header with a GUID value. The terminal logs show correlation IDs paired with request paths, confirming the middleware is executing correctly.

items.text: I can explain the difference between inline and class-based middleware
items.hint: Inline uses a lambda; class-based is a reusable class with InvokeAsync.

items.text: I can write a class-based middleware with constructor-injected dependencies
items.hint: The constructor takes RequestDelegate plus any services like ILogger<T>.

items.text: I know why I should not inject scoped services into the middleware constructor
items.hint: Middleware is a singleton; scoped services are per-request and should be resolved inside InvokeAsync.

items.text: I can register custom middleware in Program.cs
items.hint: Use app.UseMiddleware<YourMiddlewareClass>() after any required built-in middleware.

items.text: I understand how the options pattern works with middleware
items.hint: Bind configuration to a class, inject IOptions<YourOptions> into the middleware constructor.

items.text: I can use context.Response.OnStarting to modify headers before the response is sent
items.hint: OnStarting registers a callback that runs just before the response headers are flushed.

blocks.title: Custom Middleware Summary
points: Custom middleware lets you add application-specific logic to the request pipeline
Inline middleware is simple but limited — use it for small, self-contained logic
Class-based middleware supports constructor injection, making it testable and reusable
Middleware classes are singletons; only inject singleton or transient services in the constructor
Use the options pattern with IOptions<T> to make middleware configurable
Response.OnStarting lets you modify headers at the last possible moment before the response is sent
blocks.takeaway: Custom middleware is the primary mechanism for adding cross-cutting concerns to your ASP.NET Core application. Class-based middleware with dependency injection is the professional approach for anything beyond trivial inline logic.
